titleStmt.title: Cutting the Unnecessary Deadlines in EDF

analytic.title: Cutting the Unnecessary Deadlines in EDF

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Together with Fixed Priority Scheduling, Earliest Deadline First (EDF) is the second leg on top of which a large portion of the research on real-time systems stands. At the heart of the EDF exact schedulability test, a pivotal role is played by the demand bound function test, which requires to evaluate whether the amount of work required to complete a set of jobs is less than or equal to the amount of time available. Such a test is checked over a set of time instants.

In this paper, it is proposed a method that cuts drastically the set of constraints to be checked. Such a method is applicable also to tasks with release offset. Notably, it is proved that such a reduced set of constraints is minimal: it is not possible to reduce the set any further without losing the sufficiency of the test. The code to make this reduction is publicly available on GitHub.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Oftentimes real-time systems are only partially specified. For example, in real-time control systems, it frequently happens that the worst-case execution time of tasks only is specified. Such a value corresponds to the worst-case execution time of the control task, which can be determined by static analysis. When this happens, periods and possibly deadlines are free variables that the designer may choose to optimize control performance (stability, minimization of LQG/LQR control cost or else) [8], [16], [20], [21].

Conversely, there are many circumstances in which periods and deadlines are known, while the execution time of tasks may be tuned at later design phases. For example, in the imprecise computation task model [2], or in rewardbased scheduling [9], the accuracy of the application can be traded vs. the amount of computing capacity assigned to each task. The most classic application belonging to this bin is probably multimedia, where the accuracy of the rendered image/video may be finely tuned at the price of varying the task execution time. Moreover, Dynamic Voltage-Frequency Scaling (DVFS) may be casted as a problem in which the execution time of tasks may vary [11].
The schedulability of sets of tasks which are partially specified is challenging. This is sometime called sensitivity analysis. One of the aims of sensitivity analysis is to

Copyright notice: 978-1-7281-3197-9/19/$31.00 c 2019 IEEE determine the maximum/minimum tolerable values of some unspecified (or unrefined) task parameters. One approach to address sensitivity analysis is to apply binary search to the schedulability test [7], [10], [19]: if the task set is schedulable, then the computing requirement of the task of interest is incremented, otherwise it is decremented. Other approaches [15], [18] focused instead on the determination of the analytic relationships among the design parameters. By doing so, the design problem can be formulated as an optimization procedure driven by the design goal.

Contribution of this paper. This paper characterizes the feasible execution times of an EDF-scheduled set of tasks by using the minimal set of constraints. The methods here developed are implemented in C code and publicly available on GitHub 1 .

Related works. Zhang and Burns proposed the Quick convergence Processor-demand Analysis (QPA) [19]. The idea of QPA is simple and, most important of all, very effective. The demand bound function dbf(t) is tested starting from a large time instant t * and then it is evaluated backward at dbf(t * ), and so on, recursively. QPA shows an impressive reduction in the number evaluations of dbf(t). Still, the present research does not focus on offering an even faster test for EDF. Rather the focus is on: (i) the detection of the absolute deadlines which are redundant, and (ii) enabling a more effective sensitivity analysis.

In about the same years, George and Hermant did address the problem from the same perspective as made here [18]. They proposed to solve an instance of a LP problem for each absolute deadline. As shown in their paper, however, their method is not capable to automatically cut all unnecessary deadlines.

The problem of reducing the number constraints to be checked was indeed addressed by the community [3], [5]. In these approaches, it was exploited the fact that if the total utilization is bounded by some U , then all tests of the demand bound function will be true after some instant that grows with 1/(1 -U ). Instead, in this paper we aim at reducing the number of deadlines to be checked ignoring the information about utilizations.

Ekberg and Yi [22] proved that checking the EDFschedulability of a set of n tasks is (weakly) coNP-complete, even if the task set has total utilization bounded by some constant in (0, 1). We underline that the simplification of the exact test proposed here does not contradict the proved complexity of EDF-schedulability. Rather, we focus on mov-ing the complexity onto the processing of a smaller set of constraints. By doing so, the check of the constraints itself may be made more efficiently.

The problem of determining the region of EDF-feasible deadlines for given execution times and periods was also addressed [13], [14], [17]. However, in this work, we assume opposite hypothesis: periods and deadlines are known, while execution times are not.

div.head: Terminology, notation, and background
div.p: We consider a set T of n tasks. Each task, denoted by τ i , releases a sequence of jobs over time. The j-th job of τ i is released at time r i,j . We consider a sporadic task model, that is the release of two consecutive jobs belonging to the same task, is bound by the following relationship
div.formula: ∀j ≥ 1, r i,j+1 ≥ r i,j + T i ,
div.p: with T i being the minimum interarrival time of task τ i (since in this paper, the analysis of the sporadic task model coincides with the analysis of the periodic task model in which the above inequality holds with the equal sign, we often use the term period for T i ). All jobs belonging to τ i require to execute at most C i time units, which is then called worst-case execution time (or WCET) of the task (for brevity, we may drop "worst-case" and call C i as the execution time of the task). The j-th job of τ i must complete not later than D i time units after its release r i,j . D i is called relative deadline or, sometimes, simply deadline of task τ i , while the quantity d i,j = r i,j + D i is called absolute deadline of the j-th job of τ i . In the literature, three different deadline models are used
div.formula: • implicit deadlines if D i = T i , • constrained deadlines if D i ≤ T i , or
div.p: • arbitrary deadlines if the deadlines are not constrained.
In this paper, arbitrary deadlines are assumed.

The execution times C i and deadlines D i are assumed real-valued. The periods T i , instead, are assumed to be integers. In fact, periods are often multiple of some temporal unit (for example, one microsecond). This enables the definition of the hyperperiod of the task set T as

that is the least common multiple of the periods of the n tasks. The hyperperiod H has a relevant role in the schedule of real-time tasks, since the schedule of periodic tasks repeats after H time units.

Another relevant feature related to the task τ i is its utilization U i = Ci Ti . It represents the fraction of time that is required by the task to execute. The sum of all the task utilizations U = n i=1 U i is the total utilization of the task set.

We may use the vector notation for the same characteristic of all the n tasks. Hence, we use: We consider the set T of n tasks to be scheduled by the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm (also called Deadline Driven Scheduling Algorithm in early papers [1,Section 7]) over a single processor. EDF assigns the highest priority to the job which has the earliest absolute deadline d i,j . If two jobs have the same absolute deadline, the tie is broken arbitrarily. Also, we assume that the scheduler is preemptive: any job may be preempted by higher priority ones which may be released while the job is scheduled.

If the n tasks in T are scheduled by preemptive EDF, the following condition is necessary and sufficient to ensure that no job deadline is missed. Theorem 1 (Corollary 1 in [3]). The task set T is scheduled by preemptive EDF if and only if

div.p: The LHS of Eq. ( 3) is a very frequently used function in real-time EDF scheduling, and it is called demand bound function dbf(t).

Since dbf(t) is piecewise constant, the inequality of Eq. ( 3) needs to be checked only at the instants t when the dbf(t) changes value, which are all the absolute deadlines of any job. Hence, the exact condition of Theorem 1 can be simplified as stated in next corollary.

Over time, the scientific community has attacked the problem of reducing the complexity of the EDF exact schedulability test from different angles. For example [3], [5], methods exist that cut deadlines larger some boundary L, with L being an increasing function of 1/(1 -U ). These methods, however, exploit the additional information of the task set total utilization U . Since absolute deadlines depend on periods T i and deadlines D i only, a reasonable question to ask it: how many unnecessary deadlines may be cut from the set dlSet without losing the exactness of the schedulability tests?
This is the research question being addressed and answered in this paper.

div.head: Exploiting the convex hull
div.p: The set of absolute deadline of (6) will be reduced by exploiting the notion of convex hull among vectors in R n . To achieve this goal, the first necessary step is to rewrite the exact schedulability condition of Corollary 1 in a more convenient form. Equation (5), that is the test of the dbf(t), can be rewritten as
div.formula: n i=1 η i (t) t T i U i ≤ 1
div.p: or, equivalently, in vector notation as
div.formula: a(t) • U ≤ 1 with a(t) = η1(t) t T 1 η2(t) t T 2 • • • ηn(t) t T n ∈ R n . (8) Now, if we define the following finite set of vectors in R n as A = {1} ∪ {a(t) : t ∈ dlSet}(9)
with 1 = 1 1 • • • 1 ∈ R n , then the Corollary 1,
div.p: which states the necessary and sufficient EDF schedulability condition, can be equivalently (and more elegantly) stated as ∀a i ∈ A, a i • U ≤ 1 (10) with A ⊂ R n properly defined by ( 9) and ( 8). We remark that the set A of vectors includes both the vector 1, needed to enforce the total utilization constraint of Eq. ( 4), and all vectors a(t) corresponding to each absolute deadline in t ∈ dlSet, which are needed to enforce the demand bound function condition of (5).

The determination of the tightest set of constraints among the ones of (10) requires the intense application of basic linear algebra. For this purpose, we recall some basic notions on convex combinations and convex hulls. Definition 1 (convex combination). We say that a vector
x ∈ R n is a convex combination of a finite set of vectors
div.formula: {a i ∈ R n : i ∈ I}, if x = i∈I α i a i with α i ∈ R such that i∈I α i = 1, (11
div.p: and I being a finite set of indices.

The coefficients α i 's are said coefficients of the convex combination and must possess the properties of ( 11) and ( 12). Definition 2 (convex hull). We define the convex hull conv(A) of a set of vectors A = {a i } i∈I ⊆ R n as conv(A) = i∈I α i a i : a i ∈ A with the coefficients α i 's conforming to (11)- (12).

In words, the convex hull of a set A of vectors is the smallest polytope containing all vectors in A. Or, more formally, it is the the set of all convex combinations among the vectors in A. The vectors in A are called generators of conv(A).

Similarly as in vector spaces, it is interesting and useful to determine when a set of generators of a convex hull is "minimal". Next definition helps in this regard. Definition 3 (vertices of a convex hull). We say that the vectors in the non-empty set
div.formula: A V ⊆ A are the vertices of the convex hull conv(A) if ∀a ∈ A V , a / ∈ conv A \ {a}
div.p: In words, if any vector a is a vertex of conv(A) then it cannot be written as convex combination of the other vectors in A. In some sense, each vertex a ∈ A V carries a nonnegligible contribution to conv(A). Instead, vectors in A \ A V , which are not vertices, do not contribute to conv(A). The next step of the paper is to connect the exact EDF schedulability condition as written in (10), with the notions of convex hull just recalled. For this purpose, we introduce the next lemma, which is providing the right tool to cut unnecessary constraints from exact EDF-schedulability condition rewritten as in (10).

Let us now apply the just proved reduction of the number of constraints to an example. In Figure 1, it is illustrated an example of task set with constrained deadlines. Absolute deadlines of jobs are depicted by downwards-pointing red arrows, while job releases are shown by black arrows. It can be observed that the number of constraints to be checked (circled in green) drops from 51 (50 constraints from the absolute deadlines plus one on the total utilization) to 2. The constraint of i U i ≤ 1 is also redundant. In general, it can be proved that the constraint on the total utilization is always redundant, in the case of constrained deadlines.

The second example of Figure 2 has all periods and deadlines as the example of Figure 1, except D 1 which is set to 3. The task set then becomes with arbitrary deadline, since D 1 > T 1 = 2. Such a change in the deadline D 1 makes "appear" two new constraints: at t = 13 and t = 55. Moreover, the total utilization constraint is no longer implied by other constraints and it needs to be explicitly added, making the total of constraints equal to 5. In general, it can be proved that if any D i > T i , then it must be always explicitly checked that i U i ≤ 1.

A first observation is that the relevant deadlines (the ones circled in green of Figures 1 and2) tend to coincide with instants when more absolute deadlines overlap. Notably, in both examples, the time instant when the absolute deadlines of some jobs of all tasks coincide always belongs to the set of necessary deadlines (time t = 20 in Figure 1 and t = 55 in Figure 2). However, establishing a general rule does not seem trivial.
The second observation, or rather a question, is: can the set of deadlines be reduced even further? The next section answers to this second research question.

div.head: Tightness
div.p: As illustrated in the examples, Theorem 2 reduces dramatically the number of constraints to be checked for ensuring EDF schedulability. A natural question that arises at this time is whether such a set may be further reduced or not. In this section, we are going to demonstrate that the "convex hull procedure" of Theorem 2 does find the minimal set of constraints. The proof strategy is quite simple. It is proved that if any constraint with index i * which is a vertex a i * ∈ A V of the convex hull conv(A) is removed, then it is possible to find a set of utilizations U ′ which respects the constraints in A V \ {a i * } and is not EDF schedulable. That is, the test made with the constraints in A V \ {a i * } only is optimistic. The constraint of n i=1 U i ≤ 1 is not necessary, since it is implied by the constraint at t = 20. With these period and deadline parameters (hence independently of the execution times), it is necessary and sufficient to check only 2 inequalities, rather than the 50 + 1 inequalities needed by standard analysis. In this case, by applying Theorem 2, it is necessary and sufficient to check the condition only at 4 absolute deadlines (circled in green) together with n i=1 U i ≤ 1. With these period and deadline parameters (hence independently of the execution times), it is necessary and sufficient to check only 5 inequalities, rather than the 48 + 1 inequalities needed by standard analysis.

div.head: Releases with offsets
div.p: To ease the presentation, the illustrated method of computing the convex hull over vectors representing constraints is applied to a simple task model characterized by execution times C, periods T, and deadlines D. Such a method, however, may be applicable to much richer task models such as tasks with offset.

Adding the offset to the model of the task release, may allow the acceptance of more feasible task sets [6], especially in distributed systems [12]. A task τ i with a release offset is characterized by parameter, the offset φ i , which determines the sequence of job releases as follows r i,j = φ i + (j -1)T i .

Tasks with offsets are schedulable by EDF [4] if and only if By applying the same steps that transformed the exact EDF schedulability condition of Equation ( 5) into Eq. ( 10), we can transform the condition of (30) analogously. In fact, Eq. (30) can be written as
div.formula: ∀a i ∈ A, a i • U ≤ 1
div.p: (copied from Eq. ( 10)) provided that we set A = η1(t1,t2) t2-t1 T 1 • • • ηn(t1,t2) t2-t1 T n ∈ R n : t 2 = φ i + (j -1)T i + D i , t 2 ≤ 2H + max i {φ i }, t 1 = φ i + (j -1)T i , t 1 < t 2 ∪ {1}.
Hence, by computing the vertices of the set A above, the minimal set of constraints that guarantee a set of tasks with offset can be found.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, it was shown a very intimate link between the minimal set of deadline constraints that need to be checked to ensure EDF schedulability, and the convex hull of a properly defined set of vectors. The determination of such a set enables a more efficient sensitivity analysis on the execution time of tasks. We remark that we do not reduce the complexity of EDF schedulability [22]. Rather, such a complexity is moved to the off-line phase in which the deadlines are cut. Then, when it is needed to perform sensitivity analysis on the execution times of tasks, or when we aim at finding the optimal execution times of tasks that maximize some application performance, the reduced set of constraints may be used. Finally, the reduced set of deadlines is proved to be minimal, closing the case for any further reduction.

With these task parameters, by applying Theorem 2 we can find that it is necessary and sufficient to check the condition only at 2 absolute deadlines (circled in green): d 1,3 = d 3,1 = 6 and d 1,10 = d 2,4 = d 3,3 = 20.The constraint of n i=1 U i ≤ 1 is not necessary, since it is implied by the constraint at t = 20. With these period and deadline parameters (hence independently of the execution times), it is necessary and sufficient to check only 2 inequalities, rather than the 50 + 1 inequalities needed by standard analysis.
